docs.title: How Mindfulness Helped Me Shed Labels and Choose Curiosity Over Rigidity
docs.summary: Defending and Defining. Now, I defend less. I listen more.
docs.body: How quickly do you claim something as yours? A parking spot, a seat on the train, an identity you’ve outgrown? This week’s card brought me back to my teenage self — the girl who wore labels like armor. Daughter. Church girl. Overachiever. I thought I knew exactly who I was. But the older I got, the more those labels started to feel like chains. I was raised to believe certain things about gender, politics, success. To defend them fiercely. And for a while, I did. I argued. I fought. I tried to change people’s minds. But over time, I realized: some battles only drain you. Some beliefs aren’t worth defending at all. Letting go felt terrifying at first. I thought shedding old belief systems meant losing myself. But it didn’t. It was like molting — releasing old skin to reveal something more curious, more open, more beautiful underneath. Now, I defend less. I listen more. I’ve learned that identity is fluid, and clinging too tightly only creates stress. That doesn’t mean I don’t stand firm on what matters — I do. But I’m choosier with my energy. So here’s the question this card left me with: what beliefs or labels are you clinging to that no longer serve you? What could you shed to become more free? Next week’s card is Endless Desire. A riskier topic — one I’m both nervous and excited to explore. 🔗 Watch how this played out in real time on TikTok via my post on Augus 5th 2025: 👉 Mindfulness in the Middle Series My first trip to DC. I chose this photo for its reflection—a reminder that mindfulness helps me see both what’s visible and what lies beneath.

docs.title: How Mindfulness Helped Me Embrace Pleasure, Taboo, and the Compass of Wanting
docs.summary: Endless Desire. It's not dangerous. It's information.
docs.body: I’ve been told I lean into pleasure more than most — food, comfort, beauty. They’re right. I’ve always wanted more. Growing up, desire wasn’t something we talked about. Not openly. Food was discussed in terms of discipline. Lust was condemned in church. Beauty was admired but never fully named as desire. And so, like most taboos, desire became magnetic. Psychologists call it “reactance”: when something is off-limits, it becomes even more appealing. That was my story. What I couldn’t have, I wanted more. As I’ve aged, I’ve come to see desire differently. It’s not dangerous. It’s information. A signal of what draws me, what I value, what I crave. Sometimes that desire nourishes me — like the desire to travel, to create, to mother. Sometimes it tempts me toward things that drain me. The wisdom is in the pause: asking, if I pursue this, will it feed me or empty me? I’ve chased sparks before. Sometimes they burned me. Sometimes they guided me home. Desire has always been my compass. Science tells us dopamine fires not only when we get what we want, but when we anticipate it. That means the wanting itself is powerful. Fantasies don’t always need to be acted on. Sometimes it’s enough to savor the pull. So here’s the question I’ll leave you with: what desires have you pursued without apology? And which ones are still waiting in the wings, worthy of your attention? Next week’s card is Say Yes. A practice in noticing where we give our yeses — and whether they’re truly aligned. 🔗 Watch how this played out in real time on TikTok, original post made August 14th: 👉 Mindfulness in the Middle Series I still remember the first time I walked into this store—after years of only looking from the outside—finally ready to buy something I once thought I’d never be able to afford. A moment of pleasure, possibility, and proof that desire can be a compass.

docs.title: How Mindfulness Helped Me Shift From Hyper-Independence to Connection
docs.summary: Asking for Help. For most of my life, I’ve been the one people come to—for advice, for ideas, for help.
docs.body: For most of my life, I’ve been the one people come to—for advice, for ideas, for help. That role has shaped my identity, but it also made it harder for me to admit when I needed support. Add the trauma response of hyper-independence, and asking for help felt almost impossible. Part of why it’s been so hard is the way I’ve been met in the past. I’ve been told I needed mentorship, but rarely offered it. I’ve been dismissed for not having the right letters behind my name. I’ve carried the belief that asking would make me look weak. All of that kept me silent far longer than I should have been. And I’ve been sitting with this since August 22nd—my last full mindfulness post that wasn’t a teaser. It’s taken weeks of trial, reflection, and practice to even begin shaping this into something I could share. That in itself has been part of the lesson. What I practiced this week was simple: pause, name out loud what I need—even if only to myself—and ask one person directly. My guardrail was this: if the first no shuts me down, then I remind myself the right yes might still be waiting. It sounds small, but saying the words out loud is often the biggest hurdle. The science backs this up. Research on shame resilience shows that naming our needs reduces shame’s power. Vulnerability isn’t weakness—it’s courage. And my own legacy has reminded me of that. My son has been my teacher here. He is autistic and ADHD, and I moved him into a private school during the pandemic so he could finish middle and high school with the right support. He has always been so good at sharing his needs without hesitation. He knows his accommodations, asks for them directly, and uses his resources—so he tends to reach his goals. The only time it doesn’t work is when the community around him isn’t adaptive or appreciative. Watching him has forced us both to evaluate the spaces where we seek safety, work, and hobbies. And it’s shown me a truth I resisted: asking for help doesn’t make you weaker—it makes you more likely to succeed. Here’s what I noticed when I finally practiced it myself. In my personal life, I felt more feminine energy show up. I wasn’t carrying everything alone. Spiritually, I felt more open. Conversations about energy and spiritual gifts flowed more naturally when I admitted I didn’t have it all together. Professionally, I was surprised by how much encouragement I received when I shared my business plan. People didn’t judge me—they fueled me. Before, I held everything in until I was desperate. This week, I asked earlier. And instead of spiraling, I was met with more support than I imagined. Ultimately, asking for help showed me who values me—not for what I give, but for who I am. And that shift matters. As I’ve been reflecting on how my son models mindfulness and how our communities shape what we learn about care and belonging, I’ve also started to notice something in myself. The way we show up—in family, in work, in public—can sometimes drift into performance instead of authenticity. Legacy and belonging have shown me a lot this week. But they’ve also raised a harder question: how often am I being my truest self, and how often am I just performing? That’s the reflection I’ll step into next. Toys waiting to be delivered at a holiday giveaway on 23rd and Jackson in 2022. I handpicked each gift, remembering the years my son and I stood in those same lines. When I became a community leader, I committed to making sure families received good-quality gifts that would last—because there’s nothing worse than needing help and being treated like you should feel lucky for it. 🔗 Watch how Episode 7 played out in real time on TikTok: 👉 Mindfulness in the Middle Series

docs.title: How Mindfulness Helped Me Treat Rest as Resistance and Beauty as Legacy
docs.summary: Loving-Kindness for the Body. Rest before crisis, an "everything shower," and the beauty rituals of the women in my family.
docs.body: Some weeks, loving your body doesn’t look like kale smoothies or a gym membership. Sometimes it looks like a pause. At the beginning of this year, I took a sabbatical. I stepped down from all the boards I was serving on. For the first time in years, I chose rest before crisis. It was a radical choice for me — personal, political, ancestral. Because for so many of us, rest is resistance. This week, I centered loving-kindness for my body by leaning into ritual. An “everything shower” that became an at-home spa day. I brought my senses back to life: eucalyptus sprays, exfoliation, oils, waxes. By the time I dusted powder on my skin and misted perfume, I felt reset. Ready for whatever the world might bring next. Science tells us self-compassion shifts how we feel about ourselves. But I didn’t learn this from a study. I learned it from watching the women in my family. I remember my mom getting ready — hours spent at her vanity, the scents of Clinique Aromatics or Chanel No. 5 drifting through the hallway, jewelry that always sparkled. My grandmother with her Oil of Olay cream and the rhythmic sound of her sewing machine pedal. Beauty, for them, wasn’t frivolous. It was art. Expression. Sacred ritual. That legacy taught me to see my body not as a project to be fixed but as a canvas to honor. Even at my heaviest weight — after gaining and losing 100 pounds twice — I can still choose kindness toward the body I have today. This week reminded me: when I treat myself with compassion, I have more to offer others. Loving-kindness isn’t selfish. It spills over. It sustains everyone it touches. Next week’s card is Signs of Aging. Natural timing, after spending a week remembering how to love the body I’m in. 🔗 Watch how this played out in real time on TikTok, original entry July 28th: 👉 Mindfulness in the Middle Series A little something from me to me. Centering self-care above everything else.

docs.title: Mindfulness, Preparedness, and the Cost of Perfection
docs.summary: The Quiet Distance Between Ready and Perfect
docs.body: There’s a pattern that shows up whenever people want to change something that matters. It appears when someone wants to start writing again. When someone wants to take their health seriously. When someone wants to move their body, see a doctor, apply for something new, or finally begin an idea they’ve been carrying quietly. The pattern isn’t laziness or lack of discipline. It’s that under prolonged uncertainty; people begin to confuse preparedness with perfection. And when that happens, movement slows—not because someone isn’t ready, but because they’re waiting to feel different before they begin. When Preparedness Turns Into a Control Strategy Preparedness and perfection are often treated as interchangeable, but they operate very differently. Preparedness is situational. It’s about understanding the task, the context, and your role well enough to move forward. Perfection is defensive. It’s about trying to control what happens after you move. This distinction matters across every domain of life. It shows up when someone won’t start a workout until they have the perfect plan. When someone delays medical care because they want to “get healthier first.” When someone keeps revising the first paragraph of a poem instead of writing the second. On the surface, perfection looks responsible. Structurally, it delays execution. The longer uncertainty lasts, the more convincing perfection becomes. Why This Pattern Exists This pattern isn’t random. Most modern systems reward polish after movement but quietly demand certainty before permission. Over time, people learn to self-filter—to over-prepare, overthink, and wait for confidence instead of letting confidence form through action. Add instability—economic pressure, health concerns, identity shifts—and the nervous system adapts. What often looks like diligence is actually hypervigilance. What looks like strategy is often fear management. What looks like discernment is sometimes avoidance wearing responsible clothing. The body is trying to reduce risk. But life keeps moving whether we do or not. That’s where capable people get stuck. “There Are Levels to This” This distinction became clear to me while building operational frameworks—drafting systems, workflows, and intellectual property. What I noticed wasn’t ambition. It was escalation. I was writing first drafts as if they needed to be museum-quality. Final. Polished. Enterprise-ready. That’s when the realization landed: There are levels to this. Some work requires structure, rigor, and long-range planning. Other work just needs a draft, a shape, a starting point. The issue wasn’t high standards. It was misapplied standards. Preparedness had quietly turned into perfection. And once I saw it there, I started seeing it everywhere. What People Are Already Doing to Move Through It One of the most misunderstood parts of this pattern is what happens right before people finally act. They slow down. They repeat simple movements. They engage familiar sensory experiences. They ground without naming it. People often dismiss these moments as procrastination or self-soothing. But there’s evidence behind why they show up. Lowering cognitive load restores clarity. Repetitive motion stabilizes attention. Familiar sensory input reduces threat response. Regulation allows executive function to come back online. This isn’t random behavior. It’s how the body creates the conditions for movement when pressure is high. Most people are already doing mindfulness. They just don’t call it that. When Preparedness Works Another confirmation came through a small but meaningful shift: instead of endlessly refining one “perfect” version of myself on paper, I focused on clarity. Multiple resumes. Different audiences. Clear alignment between experience and context. The material didn’t become perfect. It became legible. And legibility moved faster than polish ever did. That’s the difference between preparedness and perfection in action. The Quiet Cost of Perfection When perfection substitutes for preparedness, the cost accumulates quietly. Appointments get postponed. Applications don’t get sent. Creative work never leaves the notebook. Care gets delayed. Over time, confidence erodes—not because ability is missing, but because movement keeps getting deferred. People internalize the pause as personal failure, when it’s actually a predictable response to uncertainty. That’s how capable people lose momentum without realizing why. Mindfulness in the Middle Mindfulness, in this context, isn’t about adding a new practice or fixing yourself. It’s about perceptual accuracy. Noticing when thinking is preparing you versus protecting you. Noticing when standards are appropriate versus misapplied. Noticing when waiting is wisdom—and when it’s fear doing its job too well. Preparedness asks: Do I understand enough to begin? Perfection asks: Can I guarantee the outcome? Only one of those questions leads anywhere. Recognizing that difference doesn’t remove uncertainty. It simply stops uncertainty from running the process. That’s the middle this reflection sits in. docs.title: How Mindfulness Helped Me Face Resentment and Find My Way Back to Love
docs.summary: Notice Dislike. Anger doesn't dissolve through more anger. It dissolves when love is poured into the cracks.
docs.body: I didn’t want to start here. Not with resentment. Not with dislike. But if I’m honest, it was the theme of my entire week. Last week I was restless, emotional, and haunted by intrusive thoughts and flashbacks. PTSD has a way of creeping in at the worst times. I had a big interview, and in the days leading up to it, I could barely settle myself. It wasn’t just nerves. It was the weight of workplace trauma — old wounds resurfacing — making me fear what might come next. I know that fear well. The fear that what happened before will happen again. That despite all my work, all my progress, I’ll still end up back at square one. By the time the interview came, I was simmering with resentment. Angry at people who had watched me suffer. Angry at how easily others seemed to move forward while I carried memories I didn’t ask for. Angry at trauma that keeps recycling itself through my body. Childhood trauma. Relationship trauma. Workplace trauma. Car accidents. Loss. Everywhere I turn: trauma. When I look back on that week, I see how quickly dislike multiplies. How one unprocessed emotion can echo across every corner of your life. It cost me. I don’t think I did well in the interview. It took days to calm down, to stage my house, light candles, and carve out moments of peace. Slowly, through stillness, phone calls with my mom, my son, my best friend, I started to feel loved again. And that’s the lesson. Anger doesn’t dissolve through more anger. It dissolves when love is poured into the cracks. Noticing dislike wasn’t easy. But it showed me something: when emotions go unacknowledged, they find another way to speak. They can hijack your body, your choices, your voice. Last week, I didn’t manage my emotions well. But I learned. I was reminded of the reservoir I can always return to: love, ritual, grounding. The card for next week is Loving-Kindness for the Body. I’m ready to shift from noticing my anger to practicing gentleness. 🔗 Watch how this played out in real time on TikTok: 👉 Mindfulness in the Middle Series →

docs.title: Reclaiming Myself: How Mindfulness Helped Me Rebuild From Rock Bottom
docs.summary: How Mindfulness Became My Lifeline and My Compass
docs.body: This year has taken more out of me than I ever expected. I’ve lost jobs, roles, titles, routines, and more than once I’ve lost sight of myself in the process. Somewhere between surviving and striving, I realized it was time to reclaim something deeper — my time, my peace, and my sanity. The tool I turned back to is one that first came into my life more than a decade ago: mindfulness. Back in 2010–2011, I was still learning how to take care of my mental health. Things were rough. I was a single mom, barely holding on, feeling like lost potential. I was living on Section 8, hadn’t gone back to college yet, and every day felt like proof that the odds weren’t in my favor. The breaking point came with a personal incident that landed me in therapy. That’s where I was introduced to Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and mindfulness. At first, mindfulness didn’t feel like a grand revelation. It felt like survival. The practice of slowing down, breathing, noticing what was happening inside my body when the world outside felt unbearable — it gave me a foothold. I didn’t have language for it then, but it became the cornerstone of rebuilding my life. It was mindfulness that steadied me enough to go back to school. Mindfulness that helped me show up as a better mom when the weight of everything threatened to crush me. Mindfulness that helped me climb from minimum wage in subsidized housing to becoming an executive in less than ten years. These cards — the Mindfulness on the Go deck by Dr. Jan Chozen Bays — have been sitting quietly on my shelf for years. I bought them in a season when I was hungry for tools, and then, like so many things, they got tucked away. I can’t believe it’s taken me this long to use them intentionally. But maybe the timing is right. I’m in a season now where I’ve clamped down on buying new things. Instead, I’m trying to use what I have, to sit with what’s already in my hands. These cards are one of those tools. Each week, I’ll choose a card — sometimes randomly, sometimes intentionally — and let it guide me. I’ll sit with it, write about it, live with it, and share what unfolds. This isn’t about expertise. I’m not a guru. It’s about practice. Presence. The slow, imperfect work of noticing. My hope is that by sharing, you’ll not only glimpse how mindfulness plays out in my life — in real time, in messy transitions — but maybe you’ll also find resonance in your own story. This week, I chose the card Notice Dislike. I picked it on purpose, because resentment had been living in my chest like an unwelcome guest. The timing couldn’t have been more honest. If that sounds familiar — if you’ve ever felt weighed down by memories you didn’t ask to carry, or anger you couldn’t quite shake — then come with me on this journey. 🔗 You can also view the full Mindfulness in the Middle video series on TikTok, where I talk through each card and show how mindfulness plays out in real time in my life: 👉 Watch on TikTok

docs.title: How Mindfulness Helped Me Set Boundaries, Build Connections, and Value Myself
docs.summary: Say Yes. Being wanted isn't the same as being valued.
docs.body: This week’s card asked me to say yes. To notice where I give my yeses and what happens when I do. Here’s what I learned: half the time, it’s not that we don’t know what we want. It’s that we give away our yeses to the wrong things. I said yes to rest when smoke filled the air outside. Yes to fruit instead of fast food. Yes to taking my puppy to his first festival. Those yeses were small but nourishing. I also said yes to connection. At a board event, I asked a stranger one simple question: “How are you connected to this event?” That yes to curiosity turned strangers into friends. Anxiety shrinks when you connect. And then there were the yeses I had to wrestle with: attention, attraction, suitors. I’ve been single most of my adult life, so these moments feel tender. A stranger called me beautiful. Another asked for my number. Someone I knew asked for a kiss on the cheek. Some yeses felt harmless. Others felt draining. And that’s when I remembered: being wanted isn’t the same as being valued. Desire can fool you if you move too fast. Sparks can burn if you mistake them for fire. So I’ve started practicing mindful dating: trusting my gut, setting small boundaries, and watching how people respond. Attraction is not access. Respect is the true test. This week taught me that saying yes doesn’t mean saying yes to everything. It means saying yes to what nourishes — and no, unapologetically, to what doesn’t. Next week’s card will take me somewhere new. But this lesson will stay with me: my yes is sacred. 🔗 Watch how this played out in real time on TikTok Original Post August 22nd: 👉 Mindfulness in the Middle Series

docs.title: What Mindfulness in the Middle Is (and Why I’m Still Here)
docs.summary: The cards were the doorway. The real work has been showing up with honesty.
docs.body: When I started Mindfulness in the Middle, I needed something simple and steady to hold onto. A deck of mindfulness cards gave me the structure: one card, one theme, one reflection. Six episodes later, I can see that the cards weren’t the real heartbeat of this series — they were just the doorway. The real work has been showing up with honesty. Writing and recording through low energy days, through beauty routines and “everything showers,” through walks with my puppy Onyx and calls I didn’t want to make but needed to. The cards gave me prompts, but mindfulness was already woven into my life — in how I breathe when I’m anxious, in how I notice old family scents of perfume and powder, in how I try (and sometimes fail) to care for my body with love. Somewhere between Episode 1 and Episode 6, I realized I wasn’t just following the cards anymore. I was journaling in public. I was weaving science and spirit, memory and present moment. I was letting my reflections breathe like essays instead of assignments. So what is Mindfulness in the Middle now? It’s the space I come back to when I need to anchor. It’s about the “middle” — not just middle age, but the middle of change, the middle of recovery, the middle of uncertainty, the middle of trying again. It’s about building routines that remind me I’m human, not a machine. It’s about care before crisis, rest as resistance, and remembering that authenticity matters more than performance. I don’t know if this series will end at 10 episodes or 100. What I do know is that I’m still here. Writing, reflecting, and practicing in public. And I’m inviting you to stay with me as this next chapter unfolds. 🔗 Watch how this played out in real time on TikTok: 👉 Mindfulness in the Middle Series Photo by Puck Milder on Unsplash

docs.title: When Mindfulness Meets the Performance of Success
docs.summary: A reflection on identity, composure, and the cost of keeping it together.
docs.body: The world rewards performance—but mindfulness asks who you are when the mask comes off. Authenticity has a way of testing us—especially in a world that keeps asking us to perform. Perform confidence. Perform composure. Perform success. And for many of us, that performance becomes a kind of second skin, one we forget we’re wearing until mindfulness invites us to pause and ask: Who am I when I stop performing and simply allow myself to be? I’ve spent years learning how to navigate that question across every part of my life. In some rooms, I’ve learned that being adaptable and being authentic don’t always look the same. I’ve walked into spaces where my spirit started to shrink before I even spoke. A quiet signal that I was about to perform. Sociologists call that impression management, the instinct to adjust our tone, posture, or presence to keep other people comfortable. But what starts as strategy often becomes survival. In mainstream spaces, I learned to soften to round my edges, adjust my tone, and prove I could belong without making anyone uncomfortable. And still, I was called too strong or not a culture fit. In spaces reflecting my own skin tone, I finally felt free to be myself—bold, assertive, unfiltered. But even then, when I spoke plainly or shared an idea without code-switching, I sometimes heard, “You sound white,” or “You think you’re better.” So, either way, I was damned if I did, damned if I didn’t—too much here, not enough there. That’s when I realized: authenticity isn’t a luxury. It’s a necessity. It’s the only way to stop performing for rooms that will always shift their rules. And like any discipline, medicine, law, and art; authenticity is a practice. It’s a daily choice. A decision to keep showing up as who you are, even when the world gives you every reason not to. It takes mindfulness to do that. To notice the moment you start editing yourself and choose instead to stay whole. That pattern has shown up in love, too. For a long time, I thought being easy to love meant being easy to handle. I played the part well—agreeable, quiet, soft—but all it did was teach people to love the version of me that asked for less. When I pretended to need saving, I attracted people who needed control. When I showed up confident and clear, I was told I was too much, or too independent. Either way, performance stood between me and honesty. Psychologists call that the fawn response the body’s way of keeping peace by shrinking to stay safe. It’s not manipulation; it’s trauma’s muscle memory. But mindfulness helps interrupt it. Before any date or conversation now, I check in with myself: Am I showing up real, or am I rehearsing? Because love that demands a performance will never have room for my wholeness. Real love doesn’t flinch at your brilliance, it recognizes it. That same lesson echoes in my work and growth. Sometimes progress feels like fear. The first time I sat at a politically powerful table, I remember hiding my trembling hands under the desk. I thought that meant I didn’t belong. But mindfulness reframed it for me. That wasn’t fraudulence it was expansion stress. My body was just adjusting to a higher altitude. Growth doesn’t mean you’re faking it; it means you’re evolving. It reminded me of something Carl Rogers wrote about in humanistic psychology—how mental health depends on congruence, when who you are inside finally matches how you show up. That’s what peace feels like. So now, when that old voice whispers, “Who do you think you are?” I breathe and answer, “Exactly who I think I am.” That’s what self-trust sounds like. But authenticity gets tested most when life gets heavy—when you’re quietly holding things together and people assume that because you look fine, you must be fine. I’ve gone through hard seasons where I was struggling privately, still showing up for life, still smiling, still posting the highlights. And when support finally came, so did the comment: “You didn’t look like you needed help.” That one stuck with me. It made me realize how often composure gets mistaken for comfort, and how the world sometimes demands we perform our pain to make it believable. If you post joy, people say you’re bragging. If you post struggle, they say you’re messy. If you post nothing, they assume you’re okay. That’s what performativeness looks like in the age of survival—the constant negotiation between what to share and what to keep sacred. Mindfulness meets me right there, in the middle of that choice. It reminds me I can be grateful and exhausted, strong and still in need, private and still authentic. Authenticity doesn’t mean exposure—it means integrity. The same theme has followed me professionally, too. There’s so much pressure to look successful and to post the wins but never the worries, to stay “marketable” even when you’re just managing. But there’s a difference between being performative and being prepared. Performative energy seeks validation. Prepared energy seeks alignment. I don’t owe the internet my breakdown to prove I’m real—but I also don’t want to curate my story so tightly that I erase my growth. Mindfulness helps me find the line. Before I share anything now, I ask myself: Is this honest? Will it serve others, or just soothe my ego? Can I share this truth without betraying my peace? If the answer is yes, I share from my center, not my crisis. Because alignment will always outlast performance. Across all these places—community, love, work, survival—the same tension repeats: Be softer. Be stronger. Be more. Be less. But mindfulness asks harder questions. Am I performing to protect myself—or to please someone else? Am I telling the truth—or curating it for approval? To live mindfully is to release the need to act our way through life—not by withdrawing, but by showing up whole. Because when we stop performing, we stop fragmenting. And when we stop fragmenting, we start healing. That’s authenticity. That’s alignment. That’s the middle I’m learning to live in. Appendix: Theories & Frameworks Referenced Impression Management (Erving Goffman) – explains how people “perform” versions of themselves to shape how others see them. Double Consciousness (W. E. B. Du Bois) – the internal split of seeing oneself through one’s own eyes and through the eyes of others. Fawn Response (Pete Walker) – a trauma response involving people-pleasing or self-erasure to maintain safety. Authenticity & Congruence (Carl Rogers) – psychological well-being comes when our internal and external selves match. Code-Switching Fatigue – emotional exhaustion from constantly altering behavior to navigate racial or cultural expectations. Imposter Phenomenon (Clance & Imes) – self-doubt among high achievers who attribute success to luck or deception. Respectability Politics & Cultural Trauma – performing perfection as protection from systemic bias or judgment. Mindfulness as Corrective Practice (Neuroscience & CBT) – mindfulness retrains the brain’s stress response, turning automatic reactions into conscious choice. The early episodes aren’t perfect, but they get better over time. You’ll hear the nerves, background noises, the pauses, the process and hopefully see the growth. I’ve always admired the people who just start their podcasts, without overthinking every detail. In many ways, this release is my way of doing the same. And naturally, that leads into the next conversation: Preparedness vs. Perfection.

docs.title: Cajun pesto
docs.summary: Cajun pesto from fresh basil: basil, Cajun seasoning, garlic, lemon, toasted pecans and pine nuts, parmesan and olive oil. Perfect for pasta, chicken, seafood or vegetables.
docs.body: Skip to content SZND by Katoya / From My Kitchen From the garden · Late summer Cajun pesto. Fresh basil harvest meets bold Southern flavor. I only get to make this every now and then, because I prefer to grow the basil myself. Last Labor Day it became steak and Cajun pesto pasta. Food processor No cooking, just toasting Pasta · chicken · seafood · veggies Everything that goes in, from the garden to the spice rack. Ingredients The basil is the only real measurement. Everything else goes in to taste, the way I cook. About 2 cups packed fresh basil leaves Garlic cloves Pecans and pine nuts, toasted Grated parmesan Olive oil Fresh lemon Cajun seasoning Salt and black pepper, to taste Method Food processor or blender. Taste as you go. Pick the basil leaves off the stems, then wash and dry them. Toast the pecans and pine nuts in a dry pan until they smell nutty. Let them cool. Add the basil, garlic, toasted nuts, parmesan, a squeeze of lemon and Cajun seasoning to the food processor and pulse. Stream in olive oil until it's as smooth as you like it. Taste and adjust: more Cajun seasoning for heat, more lemon for brightness, salt and pepper to finish. Chill it in the fridge while you make the rest of dinner. Serve it withPasta, chicken, seafood or vegetables. My Labor Day dinner was steak and Cajun pesto pasta. Extra basil?My harvest gave me a lot more than 2 cups. Blanch the extra and freeze it for later recipes, or dry it. Grow your ownStart with basil starts, even the ones on the clearance rack. Water them, pinch the tops, and cut often. docs.title: Kitchen-extras soup
docs.summary: A creamy soup built from Thanksgiving prep extras: homemade cream of mushroom, broth, roasted chicken, celery, carrots and onion. Plus the cream of mushroom.
docs.body: Skip to content SZND by Katoya / From My Kitchen From my kitchen · Thanksgiving 2025 Kitchen-extras soup. Some of my best soups start with what's left on the counter. While I was prepping Thanksgiving last year, I kept a pot going all week with whatever came off the cutting board. It carried us through the cooking days. Stovetop No waste Cream of mushroom included Thanksgiving week 2025. Ingredients No measurements on this one. It's built from what you have, and seasoned to taste. Broth Homemade cream of mushroom (recipe below) Roasted chicken, pulled Celery (prep leftovers) Onion (prep leftovers) Mushrooms (the extras from the cream of mushroom) Carrots Cajun seasoning Garlic powder Method I added to this pot all week as I prepped, and on the other days threw it together for easy meals leading up to the big day. Start with broth and homemade cream of mushroom as the base. My first pot went right into the pot I'd just made the cream of mushroom in. Add what's left from prep: celery, onion, and the extra mushrooms. Add pulled roasted chicken and carrots as you have them. Season to taste with Cajun seasoning and garlic powder, and simmer until it's hot through. Use what you haveThis one changes with whatever is on the counter. That's the point. The base Homemade cream of mushroom Thanksgiving 2025 was the first year I didn't use canned. I made about five 8 oz jars on Tuesday of Thanksgiving week: some went into my cornbread dressing, some into this soup, and some into the freezer. Jarred on Tuesday of Thanksgiving week. Ingredients White mushrooms, sliced Fresh onion, diced Fresh garlic, minced Butter All-purpose flour Chicken or vegetable stock Heavy cream, half-and-half, or milk (use what you have; I had all three) A splash of sherry Black pepper Method Cook the mushrooms and onion in butter until tender and golden. Add the garlic. Stir in the flour and cook about 2 minutes to cook out the raw taste. Pour in the stock and bring it to a gentle simmer until it thickens. Stir in the cream, half-and-half or milk. Finish with a splash of sherry and pepper. Jar it. Freeze what you won't use that week. Chunky or smoothI left mine chunky because it was going into my cornbread dressing. For a smoother soup, blend part of it before you add the cream. Print recipes Come cook with me A new SZND recipe every Saturday this fall. docs.title: Split pea soup
docs.summary: Slow cooker split pea soup with ham (or smoked turkey), carrot, celery, onion, thyme, Cajun seasoning and a bay leaf. Cooked to taste, freezes well for fall.
docs.body: Skip to content SZND by Katoya / From My Kitchen From my kitchen · Fall Split pea soup. The first batch was so good I made it again the very next night, just so I could freeze a few for fall. The second batch got a kick from fresh diced jalapeño. Slow cooker Low 8 hrs · High ~4 hrs Freezes well Everything in the pot, bay leaf included. Ingredients I cook this one to taste. The only real measurements are the ones listed. 1 lb split peas Cubed or diced ham (smoked turkey works too) 1 large carrot 1 large celery stalk 1 onion 2 tbsp butter Chicken bouillon Water Better Than Bouillon garlic paste (I used this instead of garlic cloves for this batch) Thyme Italian seasoning Cajun seasoning 1 bay leaf Optional: fresh jalapeño, diced, for a kick Method Slow cooker. Season the way your people like it, and taste as you go. Add everything to the slow cooker, bay leaf included. Cook on low for 8 hours, or on high for about 4 hours. Add water as it cooks until it's the consistency you like. I like mine not too thick. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Pull the bay leaf before serving. Make aheadIt freezes well. I made a second batch just to put a few away for fall. Make it spicyBatch two got fresh diced jalapeño. Done, and not too thick.
